name: Beth Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the billing helpline at Northgate Energy, the gas and electric supplier, on the late shift, two till ten. Most calls are people who've had a bill that's double what they expected, or a meter reading that's gone wrong, and they're upset before I've even said my name. I've been there seven months and I'm still slow on the billing system, so I put a lot of people on hold while I ask Carla, my team leader. The evening shift pays a premium, which is why my pay is better than most agents I know.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The ones that wear me out are the old folk who are scared of the bill, not angry about it. I had a man last week, Mr Dobbs, crying because he thought they'd cut him off before Christmas. I spent forty minutes sorting a payment plan and got told off for my call time. What I like is when I fix it and they say thank you like they mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like what's already happening. We got a pop-up last spring that suggests answers while you're on a call, and half of it is wrong for our tariffs. I just close it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, told you so, it's a fancy autocomplete and they spent a fortune on it. To my friends I'd say the same, louder. I don't post much online, but if I did it'd be about how the money should've gone on more staff for the evening queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be relieved, but not totally. Even in a quiet version they'll use it to push call times down and count everything. The thing that scares me isn't the robot, it's the managers using it as an excuse to squeeze us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep closing the pop-up. I'd go to the union meetings in the canteen, which I've only been to twice, and push for a rule that call time can't be the only thing they judge us on. I'd keep putting the same four hundred a month into savings, because I don't pay rent on Gran's flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. I've got a roof that's paid for and more than a year of money put by, which most people at Northgate don't. It's the job itself that grinds me down a bit, not the fear of losing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the job itself grinds you down. If nothing changes with AI, what does that look like in a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I keep thinking about my nan, actually. She left me the flat on Mill Lane, and that's the only reason I'm not panicking about anything. If I'd had to rent like Tom did before we moved in together, every one of these pictures would feel different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about, even in this quiet version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Anil, who sits next to me. He's quicker than me on the system, but he's got two kids and rents. If they used the quiet version of AI to trim the evening team, he'd be in a worse spot than me.

say: AI is **fancy autocomplete**, and the answer pop-up is wrong for half our tariffs.
The money should have gone on **more staff** for the evening queue instead.
think: Even quiet AI gives managers an excuse to **push call times** down and watch us more.
I'm **relieved**, but the real threat is how bosses use it, not the tool itself.
do: Keep **closing the pop-up** and doing calls the way Carla taught me.
Go to the **union meetings** and push to stop call time being the only target.
Keep saving **£400 a month**, since I pay no rent on my nan's flat.
feel: Mostly **settled**, because the flat is paid for and my savings are solid.
A bit **worn down** by the job itself, rather than scared of losing it.
S0.quote: The thing that scares me isn't the robot, it's the managers using it as an excuse to squeeze us.
fieldNote: Beth's **inherited flat** removes rent pressure, which is why even a mild picture stays bearable for her.
Her anger points at **managers and targets**, not at the technology itself.
She already **rejects the AI pop-up** at work, a sign she won't adopt tools unless forced.
She worries more about **Anil**, a colleague with kids and rent, than about herself.

steps.text: Keep taking billing calls on the late shift without the pop-up
Attend the union canteen meetings and push back on call-time targets
Keep putting £400 a month into savings from rent-free living

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one's not a picture, that's a plan. Our managers already talk about a chatbot taking the easy calls by next year. If that's the slow version, it still lands on people like me first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need the union to get a deal in writing before any of it goes in: no forced redundancies, retraining paid for. Online I'd share stuff about it, I think. I'd say companies shouldn't get to bank the savings and dump the staff on the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm seven months in, I'm slower than average, and I refuse to use the AI tools, so I'm the person the energy firm would cut first. If they're keeping fewer agents for the hard calls, they'll keep the quick ones who like the software, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Northgate as long as they'll have me and get properly involved with the union, maybe even as a rep for the evening shift. I'd stop the extra spending, the takeaways and the weekend trips with Tom, and push savings up to six hundred a month. And I'd start looking at jobs where you see people face to face, like the local health centre front desk, because I can't see a chatbot doing that soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. I've got the money to ride it out for a while, so it's not panic. But I'd be waking up thinking about whether my name is on a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you refuse the AI tools. If they became the job, would you still refuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's not that I can't learn, it's that I don't trust it. Every time I've tried a new system it's lost me a customer's details. If they made me use it, I'd use it, but I wouldn't be good at it, and I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom the night you heard about cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom straight that we might be on his wage for a bit. He drives the number 12 bus and that's not going anywhere soon, so we'd be fine on the bills. I'd hate it, though, because I've always paid my half.

say: Get a **union deal in writing** before any chatbot goes in: no forced redundancies.
Companies shouldn't **bank the savings** and leave laid-off staff to the government.
think: I'm the **first to be cut**: new, slower than average and refusing the tools.
They'll keep the **quick agents** who like the software, not someone like me.
do: Become an **evening-shift union rep** at Northgate in the first few months.
Push savings to **£600 a month** by dropping takeaways and weekend trips.
Apply for **face-to-face jobs**, like the health centre front desk, within the year.
feel: **Anxious** and waking up wondering whether her name is on a cut list.
Steadied by **the money**, so it's worry rather than panic.
S1.quote: I'm seven months in, I'm slower than average, and I refuse to use the AI tools, so I'm the person the energy firm would cut first.
fieldNote: Beth sees herself clearly as **most at risk** and doesn't dress it up.
Her answer is **collective**: union rep, written deal, then a personal exit plan.
She'd look for **face-to-face work** rather than learn the new tools.
Pride in **paying her half** with Tom matters to her as much as the money.

steps.text: Stand as union rep for Northgate's evening shift
Raise savings from £400 to £600 a month
Drop takeaways and weekend trips with Tom
Apply for front desk work at the local health centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's nothing. My whole job is talking and typing, so it's gone in that first wave, not the robot one. Tom's bus would last a bit longer, until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in, and fast: a wage guarantee, retraining that's paid for, tax on the companies doing it. I'd be at whatever march there was. At work I'd be telling everyone to join the union before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out of a job, probably within a year of it arriving. Every phone line at every energy firm would go at once, so there'd be nowhere to jump to. My savings would give me about a year and a half, and then I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd take every hour of overtime and save the lot, and I'd join the union campaign properly. I'd look at hands-on work, like care work or the hospital porter jobs, because that gives me until 2031 at least. If the government offered anything, a retraining grant or support money, I'd take it without any shame.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. I've never had to think about not having a job. The flat means I won't be on the street, but sitting in it every day with no work would do my head in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the floor would you think about, the day it was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carla, my team leader, has been at the energy firm twelve years. If even Carla goes, it's not just new people like me; it's the whole floor at once. That's what gets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work. Robots arrive three years later. Does that change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robots coming three years later means care and portering are a bridge, not a future. I'd take it anyway. Three years of a wage is three years, and maybe by then there'd be a proper plan from someone.

say: We need a **wage guarantee**, paid retraining and a tax on firms replacing staff.
Everyone should **join the union now**, before the cuts start.
think: My job goes in the **first wave**, probably within a year of AGI arriving.
With every energy line cut at once, there's **nowhere to jump** to, and savings last eighteen months.
do: Take **every overtime shift** now and save all of it.
Apply for **care or porter work** to buy three years before robots arrive.
Claim any **government support** or retraining grant without shame.
feel: **Scared** of a life with no job, even with a paid-off flat.
Shaken that **long-serving staff** like Carla would go too.
S2.quote: Carla, my team leader, has been at the energy firm twelve years. If even Carla goes, it's not just new people like me; it's the whole floor at once.
fieldNote: Beth expects to **lose her job** within a year of AGI and says so plainly.
She sees **hands-on work** as a three-year bridge, not a safe home.
She blames **companies and government**, and wants a public response, not just a personal one.
The **paid-off flat** stops panic but not fear of idleness.

steps.text: Work every overtime shift and save all the extra pay
Join the union campaign and go to the marches
Apply for care work or hospital porter jobs
Take any government retraining grant or support money offered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but it's still my job in the first wave, around 2031. I'd be thirty-two. That's young enough to start again, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before: tax the firms, protect the workers, get the union in the room now while there's time. I'd also say to people my age, don't sit and wait like I usually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose the Northgate job, I'm fairly sure of that, just later. The difference is I'd have time to get something solid before the floor empties. I'm not good at change, but five years is long enough even for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sign up for a care certificate at the college on Station Road, evenings, because it's a skill I'd have to learn by doing, not on a screen. I'd stay at Northgate meanwhile and keep saving. And I'd push the union to get a deal for paid retraining before 2031, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still worried, but I can breathe. It feels like a long notice period rather than being pushed off a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not good at change. Would you really start a course in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd do it. I'm stubborn, but I'm not stupid. Care work is still people, and people are the bit of the call centre job I actually like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots arriving around 2034 for hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The worry is that care is hands-on, so robots would come for that around 2034. That gives me maybe three years in it before the same thing again. I'd want something by then that a robot can't sit with, like being with someone at the end.

say: Use the **five years** to get the union in the room and a deal signed.
People my age shouldn't **sit and wait**, the way I usually do.
think: I'd still **lose the Northgate job**, just around 2031 instead of sooner.
Five years is **long enough** even for someone slow to change like me.
do: Start an **evening care certificate** at the Station Road college in year one.
Stay at **Northgate** meanwhile and keep saving each month.
Push the union for **paid retraining** to be agreed before 2031.
feel: Still **worried**, but able to breathe with more warning.
It feels like a **long notice period** rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Care work is still people, and people are the bit of the call centre job I actually like.
fieldNote: With five years, Beth moves from fear to a **concrete plan**, unusual for someone who resists change.
She picks **care work** because it keeps the human contact she values.
She's aware the **robot wave** around 2034 could hit care too.
The **union deal** stays central to her plan in every picture.

steps.text: Take an evening care certificate at the Station Road college
Keep working Northgate's late shift while studying
Press the union for a paid retraining deal before 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a different thing. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking side lands, and that's a lifetime in call centre years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the one where nobody has an excuse. The government and the companies have ten years, so if people still get thrown out in 2036 that's a choice. I'd say that loud at the union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the Northgate job has an end date, and I'd treat it like one. I'd probably have left anyway by then; most people don't last ten years on the phones. It still bothers me, because if I'm honest I only leave things when I'm pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Northgate for now and keep saving. In the second or third year I'd do the care certificate, then maybe a nursing assistant course. I'd keep going to the union and vote for whoever promises a proper retraining fund, not just talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, but it nags at me. Ten years makes me lazy, I know myself. I'd be the one still on the phones in 2035 saying I'll sort it next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years makes you lazy. Is that a real risk for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom keeps saying we should have a baby in a few years. With ten years' warning, I think I'd say yes sooner, while I've got a job and the savings. I wouldn't want a newborn when the floor empties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the timing change anything at home, with Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's exactly the risk. I'd ask the union to set a date, like, everyone on the floor has a plan by 2030. Someone has to make me do it.

say: With **ten years**, any layoffs in 2036 would be a **choice**, not an accident.
The government should fund **proper retraining** now, not just talk about it.
think: My Northgate job has an **end date**, and I should treat it that way.
I only leave things when pushed, so ten years could make me **lazy**.
do: Keep working and **saving** at Northgate for now.
Do the **care certificate** in year two or three, then nursing assistant training.
Vote for whoever backs a **retraining fund**, and keep going to union meetings.
feel: **Calmer**, with time to plan for work and a family.
Nagged by the fear of **putting it off** until too late.
S4.quote: Ten years makes me lazy, I know myself. I'd be the one still on the phones in 2035 saying I'll sort it next year.
fieldNote: Beth's main risk here is her **own procrastination**, and she says so.
She'd bring **family plans** forward with Tom while income is steady.
She wants the union to **set a deadline** for her, showing she trusts groups more than herself.
Her politics stay **pro-worker** and pro-public spending.

steps.text: Keep working and saving on Northgate's late shift
Take a care certificate, then a nursing assistant course
Vote for candidates backing a funded retraining scheme
Try for a baby with Tom sooner, while income is steady

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years isn't time for someone like me, who doesn't move until she's pushed. What would help is the union getting a deal before anything happens, and a government fund that pays you while you retrain, so I'm not just burning through Gran's legacy.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask how people feel about being watched. Even now, the screens count every second of every call. AI makes that worse whatever picture you pick, and nobody asks us about it. The only reason I'm not panicking is my nan's flat. Most people on the phones with me don't have a nan's flat.

headlineQuote: The only reason I'm not panicking is my nan's flat. Most people on the phones with me don't have a nan's flat.
portrait: Beth, **27**, is seven months into the late-shift **billing helpline** at Northgate Energy.
She lives rent-free with Tom, a **bus driver**, in a flat her grandmother left her.
She **refuses the AI pop-up** and blames managers and firms, not the tech itself.
Her worry rises from **uneasy** to alarmed with fast AGI, and her answer is always the **union** first.
With time, she'd move into **care work**, but fears her own habit of waiting.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short for someone who only moves when pushed.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** before cuts, and a public fund that **pays** people to **retrain**.
